title: What are the different `OutOfMemoryError` types (Java heap space, GC overhead limit exceeded, Metaspace, Direct buffer memory, unable to create native thread, Compressed class space), and what does each indicate?
shortTitle: What are the different OutOfMemoryError types, and what does each indicate?

s1_definition.profdef: `OutOfMemoryError` is a `Throwable` the JVM raises when it cannot satisfy a memory request, and its message identifies which memory region ran out. "Java heap space" means the object heap is full and GC cannot reclaim enough. "GC overhead limit exceeded" means the JVM spends almost all its time collecting and reclaims almost nothing. "Metaspace" means the native memory holding class metadata is exhausted, usually from loading too many classes. "Direct buffer memory" means off-heap NIO direct buffers exceeded their limit. "unable to create native thread" means the OS refused a new thread, typically from too many threads or OS limits. "Compressed class space" means the capped region for compressed class pointers is full.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's building running out of a specific kind of space. "Java heap space" is the main vault being full of cash boxes with nowhere to put a new one. "GC overhead limit exceeded" is the cleaning crew working around the clock but barely clearing any room, so the manager gives up. "Metaspace" is the filing room for the rulebooks (class definitions) overflowing because someone keeps printing new rulebooks. "Direct buffer memory" is the external warehouse (off-heap) hitting its cap. "unable to create native thread" is the HR office refusing to hire another teller because the building's limit is reached. "Compressed class space" is a small shelf reserved for short address labels filling up.
s1_definition.oneliner: Every OutOfMemoryError names the region that ran out, and knowing whether it is heap, Metaspace, direct memory, threads, or compressed class space tells you exactly where to look.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `OutOfMemoryError` is a `Throwable` the JVM raises when it cannot satisfy a memory request, and its message identifies which memory region ran out. "Java heap space" means the object heap is full and GC cannot reclaim enough. "GC overhead limit exceeded" means the JVM spends almost all its time collecting and reclaims almost nothing. "Metaspace" means the native memory holding class metadata is exhausted, usually from loading too many classes. "Direct buffer memory" means off-heap NIO direct buffers exceeded their limit. "unable to create native thread" means the OS refused a new thread, typically from too many threads or OS limits. "Compressed class space" means the capped region for compressed class pointers is full.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India's building running out of a specific kind of space. "Java heap space" is the main vault being full of cash boxes with nowhere to put a new one. "GC overhead limit exceeded" is the cleaning crew working around the clock but barely clearing any room, so the manager gives up. "Metaspace" is the filing room for the rulebooks (class definitions) overflowing because someone keeps printing new rulebooks. "Direct buffer memory" is the external warehouse (off-heap) hitting its cap. "unable to create native thread" is the HR office refusing to hire another teller because the building's limit is reached. "Compressed class space" is a small shelf reserved for short address labels filling up.

**One line to remember:** Every OutOfMemoryError names the region that ran out, and knowing whether it is heap, Metaspace, direct memory, threads, or compressed class space tells you exactly where to look.

sections.s2_technical:
"java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space" means the heap, where your objects live, is full and the garbage collector cannot free enough to satisfy an allocation. The cause is usually a genuine leak, holding references you no longer need, or simply an undersized heap for the real workload. You confirm it with a heap dump and the `-Xmx` setting, and you fix it by finding the retained references or raising the heap.

"java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded" is a specific signal from the throughput collector that it spent over 98 percent of time in GC while recovering less than 2 percent of the heap. It is effectively a near-full heap that keeps thrashing, so the JVM throws early instead of crawling. The fix is the same investigation as heap space, because the root cause is almost always the same, plus you can disable the check but that only hides the symptom.

"java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace" means the native region storing class metadata is full. Since Java 8 this replaced PermGen and grows in native memory, so the usual cause is a classloader leak, often from repeated redeploys in an app server or heavy dynamic class generation by frameworks and proxies. You cap it with `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` and diagnose it by watching loaded class counts; a steadily rising class count across redeploys points to a classloader leak. "java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory" means off-heap direct `ByteBuffer`s, used by NIO, Netty, and some serializers, exceeded `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize`. These buffers are freed only when their owning objects are collected and their cleaner runs, so a leak here is really unreleased or un-collected buffers. "java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread" is not about heap at all; the OS refused a thread, usually because the process hit a thread or memory limit, the `ulimit` on processes is too low, or each thread's stack reserved too much address space. The fix is fewer threads, pooling, smaller `-Xss`, or raising OS limits. "java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Compressed class space" means the capped space for compressed class pointers, part of Metaspace on 64-bit JVMs, is full; you raise `-XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize` or reduce the number of loaded classes. A senior nuance I always add: the message is a map, not a diagnosis. Heap and GC-overlimit point to the Java heap and need a heap dump; Metaspace and compressed class space point to classloading and need class-count tracking; direct memory and native-thread errors point to native memory and the OS, where a heap dump shows nothing, so you need Native Memory Tracking instead.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's statement service slowly fills the heap by caching every transaction it ever loaded in a static list, and one night it dies with "Java heap space." This is exactly the heap-space OutOfMemoryError — an unbounded collection retaining objects forever.

Problem 2 — A different service that redeploys frequently dies with "Metaspace," and another that downloads large statement files with NIO dies with "Direct buffer memory," while a thread-per-request design dies with "unable to create native thread" under load. This is exactly the point that each message names a different region with a different root cause and a different fix.

The demo deliberately and safely reproduces each category in a small, bounded way and logs which region failed, so the reader sees the distinct errors. Classes and steps: `HeapExhaustionDemo`, `MetaspaceNote`, `DirectBufferDemo`, `NativeThreadNote`, each triggering or explaining one category.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
oom-types-lab/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   └── main/
│       └── java/com/bank/oom/
│           ├── OomTypesDemo.java            (orchestrates the safe demos)
│           ├── HeapExhaustionDemo.java      (Java heap space)
│           ├── DirectBufferDemo.java        (Direct buffer memory)
│           └── NativeThreadDemo.java        (unable to create native thread)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run with small limits so each region fills quickly and safely
java -Xmx128m -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m -cp target/classes com.bank.oom.OomTypesDemo

# Capture a heap dump automatically on a REAL heap OOM in production
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps -jar app.jar

# Inspect NATIVE memory (direct buffers, threads) where a heap dump shows nothing
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a run with a 128 MB heap and a 128 MB direct memory cap, exercising each category.

Step 1 — The demo prints the explanations for Metaspace, Compressed class space, and GC overhead limit exceeded, because those are classloading and GC-thrashing conditions better explained than forced in a tiny demo.

Step 2 — HeapExhaustionDemo keeps adding large arrays to a static list that is never cleared, so the heap fills and the JVM throws "Java heap space." The demo catches it, logs that this is a heap condition needing a heap dump, and clears the list so the JVM survives.

Step 3 — DirectBufferDemo allocates 16 MB direct buffers and keeps references so they are never freed, exceeding the direct memory cap, and the JVM throws "Direct buffer memory." The demo logs that this is off-heap and invisible to a heap dump, needing Native Memory Tracking instead.

Step 4 — NativeThreadDemo starts threads until the OS refuses, and the JVM throws "unable to create native thread." The demo logs that this is an OS thread limit, not a heap problem, fixed by pooling, a smaller stack size, higher ulimits, or virtual threads, then releases the threads.

```
2026-10-26 15:45:01 [INFO] Metaspace OOM → native class-metadata region full ...
2026-10-26 15:45:01 [INFO] GC overhead limit exceeded → >98% time in GC ...
2026-10-26 15:45:02 [SEVERE] CAUGHT: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space → heap full ...
2026-10-26 15:45:03 [SEVERE] CAUGHT: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory → off-heap ...
2026-10-26 15:45:04 [SEVERE] CAUGHT: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread → OS limit ...
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  JVM Process Memory
  ├── Heap (-Xmx) ───────────────► "Java heap space"  /  "GC overhead limit exceeded"
  │     objects, caches             cause: leak or undersized heap  → heap dump + MAT
  │
  ├── Metaspace (native) ────────► "Metaspace"
  │     class metadata              cause: classloader leak / dynamic classes → class count
  │     └─ Compressed class space ► "Compressed class space"
  │          class pointers          cause: too many classes → -XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize
  │
  ├── Direct/NIO memory (native) ► "Direct buffer memory"
  │     DirectByteBuffer, Netty      cause: un-freed buffers → NMT, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize
  │
  └── Thread stacks + OS ─────────► "unable to create native thread"
        one native thread each       cause: too many threads / ulimit → pool, -Xss, vthreads

  Rule: message names the REGION → tells you which tool to use.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — OOM Type → Region → Tool ═══

  ┌─ Mapping (as prose) ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Java heap space        : heap full/leak    → heap dump + MAT   │
  │ GC overhead limit      : heap thrash       → heap dump + MAT   │
  │ Metaspace              : classloader leak  → loaded-class count│
  │ Compressed class space : too many classes  → CompressedClassSz │
  │ Direct buffer memory   : off-heap buffers  → NMT, MaxDirectMem │
  │ unable to create thread: OS thread limit   → pool, -Xss, ulimit│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: each demo reproduces exactly ONE region's exhaustion        │
  │ O: add a new demo class per new region, no edits to others     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Decision Flow ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  OOM message?
    ├─ "Java heap space"/"GC overhead"  → heap dump → find retained refs
    ├─ "Metaspace"/"Compressed class"   → track loaded classes → classloader leak
    ├─ "Direct buffer memory"           → NMT → un-freed DirectByteBuffer
    └─ "unable to create native thread" → thread count/ulimit → pool/vthreads
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
OutOfMemoryError is thrown when the JVM cannot satisfy a memory request, and the key insight I always lead with is that the message names the exact region that ran out, so the message is really a map telling me which tool to reach for. Java heap space means the object heap is full, either from a genuine leak where I am holding references I no longer need, or simply from an undersized heap for the real workload, and I diagnose it with a heap dump and the MAT tool. GC overhead limit exceeded is a closely related signal from the throughput collector that it is spending over ninety-eight percent of its time collecting while recovering almost nothing, so it throws early instead of crawling; the root cause and the fix are the same as heap space.

Metaspace means the native region that stores class metadata is full, which since Java 8 lives in native memory, and the usual cause is a classloader leak from repeated redeploys or heavy dynamic class generation by proxies and frameworks, so I cap it with MaxMetaspaceSize and diagnose it by watching the loaded-class count rise. Compressed class space is a capped sub-region for compressed class pointers on sixty-four-bit JVMs, and when it fills I either raise CompressedClassSpaceSize or reduce how many classes I load.

Direct buffer memory is completely different because it is off-heap: NIO and Netty allocate direct ByteBuffers outside the heap, and when they exceed MaxDirectMemorySize or are not released I get this error, and crucially a heap dump shows me nothing, so I use Native Memory Tracking instead. Unable to create native thread is not about memory regions inside the JVM at all; the operating system refused a new thread because I hit a thread or process limit, the ulimit is too low, or each thread's stack reserved too much address space, and the fix is to pool threads, lower the stack size, raise OS limits, or move to virtual threads.

In my banking work at National Bank of India I have seen each of these in production. The statement service died with Java heap space because a static list cached every transaction forever, which a heap dump in MAT pinpointed immediately. A frequently redeployed service died with Metaspace from a classloader leak, a file-download path died with Direct buffer memory from un-freed NIO buffers that only Native Memory Tracking revealed, and an old thread-per-request design died with unable to create native thread under load, which we fixed by pooling. The senior point I always close with is that heap and GC-overlimit errors need a heap dump, Metaspace and compressed-class errors need class-count tracking, and direct-memory and native-thread errors need Native Memory Tracking and the OS view, because a heap dump is blind to native memory.
